previous_admission_summary.summary_paragraph: A woman with a history of polymyositis, morbid obesity, type 2 diabetes, chronic venous thromboembolism, interstitial lung disease, and diastolic heart failure was admitted for worsening shortness of breath and URI symptoms one week after a prior discharge. She had gained 10 pounds, attributed to poor adherence to a low-sodium diet, and was treated with intravenous diuretics. Her respiratory symptoms were determined to be from a viral upper respiratory infection, not pneumonia, and antibiotics were withheld. She improved with diuresis, losing 9 pounds, and was transitioned from furosemide to torsemide for better bioavailability. Iron therapy was started for iron deficiency anemia, and warfarin was held briefly for an elevated INR before being safely restarted. She was discharged home with improved symptoms, instructions to monitor daily weights, and follow-up plans with her PCP and specialists.

#. Polymyositis: Pt currently unable to ambulate ___ weakness. 
Pt states she typically gets rituximab infusions q6-8 weeks for

infusion. Pt's case was discussed with rheumatology team. Given 
her CKs were in the 700s (rather than the 10,000s like previous 
flares), no changes were made to the patient's medications. Her 
outpt rheumatologist is continuing to work on getting rituximab 
approval. Pt states her pain typically responds well to 
ibuprofen, so this was used PRN pain. Her home dose of steroids 
and mycophenolate were continued, as was Bactrim for PCP ___.

rheum follow up and rituximab infusion when approved (will be 
arranged by rheum team).

crackles on exam, although both are limited by body habitus. No

and Guaifenesin PRN.
